title: How Teen ‘After-Prom’ Kings in LA Monetized the High School Rager
gist: MyPlots' 20%-take-rate ticketing app for LA teen parties has scaled past 1 million users and is raising a $10 million round to move upmarket into adult celebrity nightlife, while operating in an uninsurable, weakly age-gated liability gray zone that both founders openly frame as a short-term money engine rather than a long-term mission.

insights.claim: MyPlots takes a 20 percent commission on all ticket sales and has surpassed 1 million users among LA's under-21 demographic, having grown by out-executing Partiful on in-app ticketing before Partiful copied the feature and announced its own in-app ticketing in June 2026.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Shows a first-mover feature advantage in a narrow niche can be temporary once proven profitable, since larger incumbents can quickly replicate a differentiating monetization mechanic.
insights.locator: When it launched last year, the ticketing feature distinguished MyPlots

insights.claim: MyPlots is raising a $10 million angel round to fund a permanent office, a talent-booking sales team, and a planned 10,000-person festival on Santa Monica beach, indicating an ambition to move from a ticketing app into a vertically integrated live-events and festival business.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A materially larger and more capital-intensive business model than the company's origin as a peer-to-peer teen ticketing app.
insights.locator: MyPlots is in the middle of a search for angel investors

insights.claim: Multiple competing platforms and promoters, including ticketing apps Plots and Turnt and promotion outfits 310 Events, Off Campus Events, and LA Social, already operate in the same youth event-monetization space as MyPlots, indicating the category is a moderately crowded emerging sub-market rather than a single-company opportunity.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Competitive density is a relevant factor in assessing MyPlots' defensibility as it pursues its funding round.
insights.locator: In addition to MyPlots, there are promoters like 310 Events

insights.claim: Despite a nominal 18-plus age requirement, MyPlots' Stripe payment integration allows account holders as young as 13 with a parent enrolled, and the founder admits users find workarounds, an unresolved compliance gap as the platform scales into paid, alcohol-adjacent adult nightlife.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A structural age-verification gap that could draw regulatory or payments-partner scrutiny as usage and event scale grow.
insights.locator: To use MyPlots, users technically need to be 18

insights.claim: An insurance broker states plainly that once minors and alcohol combine at an event, 'no carrier will knowingly touch it,' and that contracts with minors are generally unenforceable, meaning platforms and promoters facilitating underage ticketed parties operate largely outside conventional liability coverage.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Establishes the tail-risk liability structure underlying the platform's core use case, relevant to gauging downside legal exposure for MyPlots and the promoters using it.
insights.quote: Take that same party and make everyone 21, and it’s insurable. Add minors and alcohol, and no carrier will knowingly touch it.
insights.locator: Here’s what it really comes down to

insights.claim: MyPlots founder Jack Schwartz structurally distances the company from legal liability for the parties it monetizes, stating he doesn't know '95 percent' of the promoters using his platform, offloading event risk onto individual promoters while the company still collects its 20 percent transaction cut.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A liability-shifting platform posture comparable to gig-economy intermediaries, worth tracking as a template other youth-event apps may adopt.
insights.quote: I have no idea who 95 percent of [the promoters] are
insights.locator: Schwartz wants to distance himself from promoters

insights.claim: A venue-liability source recounts an incident where a Brentwood dance studio's floor collapsed under the weight of a teen party crowd, sending 'rowdy rich kids spilling into the streets' per a Los Angeles Magazine report, illustrating the physical safety tail-risk embedded in the underinsured, informally-permitted venue model that platforms like MyPlots rely on to scale events cheaply.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A documented safety-failure incident underscoring real physical liability exposure in the teen-party venue ecosystem underlying this business.
insights.quote: rowdy rich kids spilling into the streets
insights.locator: Matt recalls that a dance studio in Brentwood

insights.claim: A parent source identifies the underlying demand mechanism: teenagers with independent mobility via ride-hailing apps and unsupervised access to parents' stored payment cards on their phones are, in her words, 'absent-mindedly spending a lot of money' on ticketed teen events.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific consumer-behavior mechanism—frictionless mobile payment plus teen independence—enabling the monetized-party economy that platforms like MyPlots depend on.
insights.quote: Kids are just kind of absent-mindedly spending a lot of money.
insights.locator: The fact that “everyone has their parents’ credit card on their phone”

insights.claim: MyPlots has expanded beyond its LA teen-party origin into adult celebrity nightlife on the East Coast, including a $27,500 table-fee after-party tied to a Madison Square Garden show and a prior Playboi Carti event, evidence of rapid upmarket migration toward higher-revenue-per-event adult nightlife promotion.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Indicates a deliberate strategic pivot toward a higher-margin, higher-visibility segment as the company seeks growth capital.
insights.locator: Schwartz and the MyPlots team are hosting an after-party

insights.claim: Even while on vacation in Ibiza, the founders printed paper flyers and threw them into a crowd outside a nightclub to promote a self-organized villa party, then charged roughly $100 per head and collected around $10,000 in a single night, illustrating how low the marginal cost is for them to convert audience reputation into cash via ticketed events.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A concrete data point on the founders' ability to rapidly monetize an audience with minimal marketing spend, relevant to assessing their execution capability outside their home market.
insights.locator: We go to this post office, we create a flyer

insights.claim: Founder Jack Schwartz says his end goal is to sell MyPlots and pivot to 'something in AI,' while cofounder Zane Harwin frames the mission as making 'as much money as I possibly can, as soon as I can,' both signaling the venture is run with an explicit near-term monetization and exit mindset rather than a long-horizon platform-building one.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Founder-stated exit intent is a material signal for evaluating how much long-term strategic commitment underlies the company's current fundraising and expansion plans.
insights.quote: Make as much money as I possibly can—as soon as I can.
insights.locator: Harwin puts the long-term goal more plainly

insights.claim: Cofounder Zane Harwin predicts the company could eventually be 'doing something bigger than Coachella,' an aspirational claim from a 19-year-old cofounder made without any operational or financial evidence cited in the piece to support the scale comparison.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: An unsubstantiated but notable growth claim from company leadership worth tracking against the company's actual festival execution (the planned Santa Monica beach event) as a reality check.
insights.quote: It’s very possible we're going to be doing something bigger than Coachella once we get older.
